title: Tip: your first dark-evening lessons
fb_text:
The clocks went back on 25 October. For some of your pupils, this week is their first lesson in the dark.

A few things that help the first one go well:

1. Tell them in advance. "Tonight we'll be driving in the dark" lets them come ready, not anxious.
2. Start on a route they already know. New roads and darkness at once is too much.
3. Do a lights check together before moving off: dipped beam, main beam and the warning light, rear lights.
4. Give their eyes a couple of minutes to adjust, and talk about not staring at oncoming headlights.
5. Point out pedestrians and cyclists early. They're much harder to spot after dark.
6. Leave time at the end to talk about how it felt.

Driving in the dark is DVSA skill 24. Our guide has more.

title: Tip: headlight rules learners get wrong
fb_text:
Five Highway Code headlight rules worth going over before your next evening lesson.

1. Use headlights at night (half an hour after sunset to half an hour before sunrise), except on roads with lit street lighting. (Rule 113)
2. Sidelights and rear number plate lights must be on between sunset and sunrise. (Rule 113)
3. Don't dazzle. In a stopped queue, once the car behind has stopped, take your foot off the brake so your brake lights don't glare. (Rule 114)
4. Keep dipped when overtaking until you're level with the other vehicle. (Rule 115)
5. Dazzled by oncoming lights? Slow down, and stop if you need to. (Rule 115)

Test prep: switching on dipped headlights ("show me") and main beam ("tell me") are both on the official list.

Save this for later.

https://driveschoolpro.com/blog/night-driving-tips/?utm_source=facebook&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=nov26&utm_content=n05

title: Tip: cutting no-shows in the dark months
fb_text:
Late cancellations go up when it's cold, dark and wet. Here's how to protect your diary this winter.

1. Write your cancellation policy down and send it to every pupil. 24 or 48 hours' notice is common for ADIs. Whatever you pick, apply it the same way to everyone.
2. Remind every lesson, every time. A reminder the day before catches most "I forgot".
3. Ask for a confirmation, not just a read receipt.
4. Agree a bad-weather plan in advance: if it's unsafe to drive, you'll move the lesson, not cancel it. Pupils relax when they know.
5. Keep a short waiting list of pupils who want extra lessons, so a gap can be filled.

Our full guide has 8 strategies.

https://driveschoolpro.com/blog/reduce-driving-lesson-no-shows/?utm_source=facebook&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=nov26&utm_content=n08

title: Tip: the 10-minute weekend admin routine
fb_text:
Ten minutes on a Sunday night saves an hour of chasing in the week.

A simple routine:

1. Look at next week's diary. Any gaps you can offer to your waiting list?
2. Check who owes you money, and send the reminders now, not mid-lesson.
3. Finish last week's lesson notes while you still remember them.
4. Check car dates: MOT, tax, insurance, service. Nothing should surprise you.
5. Block out your own time: school runs, appointments, days off.
6. Note anyone with a test coming up and plan their next lessons around it.

Do it the same time every week and it becomes automatic.

title: Tip: how the standards check is scored
fb_text:
Standards check coming up? Here's exactly how it's scored, from GOV.UK.

- The examiner watches you give a normal, client-centred lesson for about 45 minutes. Your pupil drives for about 40 of them.
- You're marked on 17 competencies in 3 groups: lesson planning, risk management, and teaching and learning skills.
- Each competency scores 0 to 3. The maximum is 51.
- 0–30 is a fail. 31–42 is Grade B. 43–51 is Grade A.
- You fail automatically if you score 7 or less in risk management, or if the examiner stops the lesson because of danger.
- Fail and you get up to 2 more attempts. Fail 3 times and you're removed from the register.

Risk management is the section to work on first.

title: Tip: winter checks for the tuition car
fb_text:
Your car is your office. Five winter checks to do this week, and a lesson for your pupil in each one.

1. Tyres: the legal minimum is 1.6mm across the central three-quarters of the tread, all the way round. Check pressures when the tyres are cold.
2. Lights: every bulb, front and back, including number plate lights. Clean the lenses.
3. Screenwash: top up with a winter mix so it doesn't freeze.
4. Clear view: before every lesson, clear all snow and ice from all windows, keep lights clean and mirrors clear (Highway Code Rule 229).
5. Paperwork: MOT, tax and insurance dates in your diary, not your head.

Tyres and lights are also "tell me" questions on the test, so get your pupil to do the checks with you.

https://driveschoolpro.com/blog/car-safety-checks/?utm_source=facebook&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=nov26&utm_content=n16

title: Tip: the mid-course wobble
fb_text:
Around the middle of a course, a lot of pupils go quiet. Lessons get "busy", gaps get longer, and some just drift away.

It's usually not you. The early wins (moving off, first roundabout) have stopped, and the last stretch to test standard feels slow.

What helps:
- Show them how far they've come. Go back to where they were on the skills at lesson one.
- Name the two or three skills between them and test-ready. A short list feels doable.
- Set a goal for the next three lessons, not "until you're ready".
- Ask, plainly: "How are you finding it?" Then listen.

Pupils who can see their progress tend to stick with it.

title: Tip: the first 3 minutes of a standards check
fb_text:
The first three minutes of your standards check set up the whole lesson.

GOV.UK says you should start by agreeing the lesson goals and how you'll manage risk with your pupil, in no more than 3 minutes. At the end, give your pupil about 3 minutes to reflect.

In between: a normal lesson that fits the pupil. You can't spend the whole lesson on a manoeuvre, but a short recap of one is fine. You can stop safely to give feedback if you need to.

A simple opener: "What would you like to work on today? Here's how we'll split who does what if something goes wrong."

In between: a normal lesson that fits the pupil. You can't spend the whole lesson on a manoeuvre, but a short recap of one is fine. You can stop safely to give feedback if you need to.

A simple opener: "What would you like to work on today? Here's how we'll split who does what if something goes wrong."

title: Tip: Road Safety Week, teaching the hierarchy of road users
fb_text:
It's Road Safety Week (15 to 21 November), and this year's theme is "Safe people on the move".

A good week to check your pupils understand the hierarchy of road users in the Highway Code. Rule H1 puts it simply: those in charge of vehicles that can cause the greatest harm bear the greatest responsibility to take care.

Three things to cover on a lesson this week:
- At a junction, give way to pedestrians crossing or waiting to cross the road you're turning into or out of (Rule H2).
- Don't cut across cyclists or horse riders when you turn (Rule H3).
- After dark, people walking and cycling are much harder to see. Look earlier and slow down sooner.

Ask your pupil to explain it back to you. If they can teach it, they've got it.

title: Tip: ice and stopping distances
fb_text:
On ice, stopping distances can be ten times longer than on a dry road. That's the one number every pupil should know this winter.

From the Highway Code:
- Wet roads: stopping distances are at least double (Rule 227). Double your two-second gap too.
- Icy or snowy roads: they can be ten times greater (Rule 230).
- Before you set off: clear all snow and ice from all windows, make sure lights are clean and mirrors are clear (Rule 229).

On a frosty morning lesson, start with the gap. Get your pupil to count "only a fool breaks the two-second rule", then talk about what ten times longer looks like on the road in front of you.

Smooth, gentle inputs on everything: steering, brakes and accelerator.

title: Tip: fog lights, on and (more often) off
fb_text:
The fog cleared half an hour ago. The rear fog light is still on, and the driver behind can't tell when you're braking.

The Highway Code is clear:
- Use headlights when visibility is seriously reduced, generally when you can't see more than 100 metres (Rule 226).
- Only use fog lights in those conditions, and switch them off when visibility improves (Rule 236). They dazzle and can hide your brake lights.

Good test prep too: "Tell me how you'd switch on the rear fog light(s) and explain when you'd use it/them" is on the official "tell me" list. Get your pupil to find the switch and the warning light.

title: Tip: what an hour of teaching really costs you
fb_text:
Before you set next year's lesson price, work out what an hour actually costs you to deliver.

1. Add up a year of business costs: car (finance or depreciation), fuel, insurance, servicing and tyres, franchise fee if you have one, phone, software, CPD, your ADI registration.
2. Count paid hours, not working hours. Travel between pupils, admin and cancellations you didn't charge for all eat into it.
3. Divide costs by paid hours. That's what each lesson costs before you've paid yourself a penny.

Example only: £12,000 of costs over 1,000 paid hours is £12 an hour gone before you earn anything.

Then decide what you need to take home, and work back to a price. Our free calculator does the sums.

title: Tip: the winter "show me tell me" questions
fb_text:
Five of the "show me tell me" questions matter most in winter. Can your pupil do them without hunting for the switch?

Show me (asked while driving):
- How you'd demist the front windscreen
- How you'd set the rear demister
- How you'd switch on your dipped headlights
- How you'd wash and clean the front (or rear) windscreen

Tell me (asked before driving):
- How you'd switch on the rear fog light(s) and when you'd use them

Getting one or both wrong is one driving fault. But driving dangerously while doing a "show me" is a fail, so practise until it's automatic and they keep their eyes on the road.

title: Tip: the 2-minute lesson recap habit
fb_text:
The last two minutes of a lesson are worth more than the two minutes before it.

Pull over somewhere safe and ask:
1. "What went well today?"
2. "What would you do differently?"
3. "What should we work on next time?"

Let them answer first. Then add your view, and agree one focus for the next lesson. Write it down, so next week starts where this one ended.

It builds the habit of reflecting, which is part of the client-centred approach DVSA looks for, and it's exactly what the examiner expects at the end of a standards check.

title: Tip: low winter sun
fb_text:
In winter the sun sits low in the sky right at school-run and home-time. Is your pupil ready for it?

- The Highway Code is short and clear: slow down, and if necessary stop, if you're dazzled by bright sunlight (Rule 93).
- Clean the inside of the windscreen. A greasy film you can't see in normal light turns into a white sheet in low sun.
- Use the sun visor early, before they're squinting.
- Leave a bigger gap. The driver in front may be dazzled too and brake suddenly.
- Remember pedestrians and cyclists can be lost in the glare.

And once the sun's gone: no tinted glasses at night (Rule 94).

title: Tip: what triggers a standards check letter
fb_text:
DVSA watches four numbers from your pupils' driving tests over a rolling 12 months. Hit three of them and you'll be asked to book a standards check.

The four triggers:
1. An average of 6 or more driving faults per test
2. An average of 0.55 or more serious faults per test
3. The examiner taking physical action on 10% or more of tests
4. A pass rate of 55% or lower

Fewer than three? You're less likely to be called, but you can still be asked in each 4-year registration period. If you bring fewer than 5 pupils to test, or don't teach learners, you must take one in each 4-year period anyway.

Ignore the letter and you can be removed from the register.
